reason: An empty fragment names the scope itself, here the package at the module root.
A package-level function, spelled by its declared name.
An unexported package-level function; case is kept as declared and nothing marks the visibility.
A package-level type; the same form names a struct, an interface, a defined type and an alias.
A package-level constant; a Go enumerated member is a package-level constant and takes this form.
A package-level variable.
A non-ASCII identifier is carried as its UTF-8 bytes, never percent-encoded and never normalized.
A test function in an in-package test file shares the production package's scope.
A test function in an external test package is scoped by that package's own path, the directory path with the _test suffix.
A symbol in a main package is scoped by the package's import path like any other.
A method is its receiver's base type name, a dot and the method name; the pointer star of the receiver never appears.
A method on a generic type names the type without its type parameters.
An interface method takes the same form as a concrete method: the interface name, a dot and the method name.

reason: A struct field always carries its struct; a field name alone would be a package-level reference.
An embedded field is spelled by its field name, which Go defines as the unqualified type name.
A field of an anonymous struct type is reached through the field that carries the type, here through a slice element.
example:
type Manifest struct {
	Tools []struct{ Name, Version string }

reason: A type parameter of a function is the function name followed by the parameter name in square brackets, Go's own instantiation syntax.

reason: A type parameter of a method follows the method's own reference.
The brackets carry the method's own type parameter; the receiver type's parameter is the type's and is not a subject.
A source file is its base name and the file selector, scoped by the import path of the directory that holds it.
A require directive is the required module path and the require selector, scoped by the module whose go.mod carries it.
A replace directive that names a version carries it after an at sign, because two replace lines for one module at two versions are distinct directives.
A replace directive with no version has no at sign.
No language prefix. Every reference starts with its language and the three characters ://, so that a Go symbol and a TypeScript symbol of one name stay distinct.
The language prefix is lowercase and compared bytewise.
Whitespace never appears in a Go reference.
A Go identifier does not start with a digit.
Percent-encoding is refused: a reference is compared as bytes and never decoded, so the non-ASCII identifier is carried as UTF-8.
No fragment separator. The package itself is spelled with a trailing #, so that a scope is never mistaken for a symbol.
An import path neither starts nor ends with a slash.
A dot-qualified shape has no fragment separator, and a path such as gopkg.in/yaml.v3.Node would split ambiguously.
The display name with its receiver star is symbol.name, never the reference; a type has at most one method of a name whatever the receiver kind, so the star carries nothing.
A parameter has no reference of its own; a finding about one carries the enclosing method's reference and names the parameter in its position and its symbol.name.
A trailing dot leaves the chain incomplete.
Members are joined by a dot. A second # is not a member separator, because # is the scope separator here.
A declaration carries no selector; the Go selectors are file, require and replace, and each names a non-code subject.
A reference never contains LF, so that it can be a line's field, a hash input separated by LF and a JSON string alike.
A reference never contains CR.
Type arguments never appear on a container; the method of a generic type is spelled List.Push.
A signature never appears; an interface method is named, not typed.
The only member separator is a dot.
Whitespace never appears in a Go reference, not even after the member separator.
A slash belongs to the import path, before the #; a field is reached from its struct with a dot.
The constraint is not part of the reference; only the type parameter's name is.
Empty brackets name no type parameter.
Type arguments never appear on a container; a method's type parameter follows List.Map and the receiver type's parameter has no reference.
A type parameter follows a function or a method, so no chain deeper than a type and its method carries one.
A selector follows its operand, after a colon, as in render_windows.go:file.
Selectors are lowercase and compared bytewise.
A require directive is spelled by its module path alone; the required version is the directive's value, not its identity, and whitespace never appears.
The go.mod keyword order is not the reference: the selector follows the module path after a colon.
exclude is not a selector: an exclude directive is never a finding subject, so it has no reference.
An empty fragment names the scope itself, here the module: a package name, then the file's path inside the package with its real extension.
An exported module-level declaration, spelled by its declared name; a value and a type of one name in one module are one symbol and one reference.
A module-level declaration that is not exported takes the same form; nothing marks the visibility.
A module-level variable.
A .tsx file is a module like any other; the extension is the file's own.
A JavaScript module is under the ts prefix, because one analyzer covers both languages and the prefix names the analyzer's language family.
A declaration file keeps its .d.ts extension.
When no manifest above the file carries a name, the package component is a single dot and the path is relative to the target root; an npm name never starts with a dot, so the two cannot collide.
A default export is spelled default, its export name; the local class name, if any, is symbol.name.
An export specifier creates an alias symbol distinct from the declaration it names; the alias selector keeps the two apart when they share a module and a name.
A renamed re-export is spelled by its exported name.
A default export written as a separate statement is an alias of the declaration it names.
An instance member is the class name, a dot and the member name; the private modifier changes nothing in the spelling.
A method is a member like a property; a getter and a setter of one name are one symbol and one reference.
A private name keeps its hash sign, which is part of the name in the language; the scope separator is the first # of the reference, so a later # is a name.
A static member always carries the static selector, because a class may declare a static and an instance member of one name.
A member whose name is not an identifier is written as a single-quoted string.
Inside a quoted component a quote, a backslash, LF and CR are escaped as \', \\, \n and \r; every other character stands for itself.
A member declared with a computed key is spelled as the key's source text in square brackets, whitespace removed.
An interface member is the interface name, a dot and the member name.
A non-ASCII identifier is carried as UTF-8 and is not quoted, because it is an identifier.
A member of the object type a type alias declares is the alias name, a dot and the member name.
example: export type Layout = { gap: number; width: number };

reason: An enum member is the enum name, a dot and the member name.
An enum member declared with a string-literal name is quoted like any other non-identifier name.
Nested namespaces are a chain of names from the module-level declaration inward.

A type parameter of a method follows the method's own reference.
On a static method the static selector comes first and the type parameter last.
A container may nest, so a method of a class inside a namespace carries its type parameter at the end of the whole chain.
